4351.stem: A coin is biased so that it is twice as likely to show a head than a tail.

parts.latex: What is the probability of obtaining a head with one throw of this coin?
In two throws of this coin, what is the probability of obtaining at least one head?

solutions.latex:
A head is twice as likely as a tail, so $P(H) = 2P(T)$. The probabilities sum to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} P(H) + P(T) &= 1 \\ 2P(T) + P(T) &= 1 \\ P(T) &= \dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(H) = \dfrac{2}{3}$$

meta.generated_note: Worked solution written from the question.

solutions.latex:
"At least one head" is the complement of "no heads" (two tails). The throws are independent, with $P(T) = \dfrac{1}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{two tails}) &= \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{9} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one head}) &= 1 - \dfrac{1}{9} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{9} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(\text{at least one head}) = \dfrac{8}{9}$$

solutions.latex:
The die has 6 faces and the spinner has 4 sections, so there are $6\times 4 = 24$ equally likely outcomes in the table.

Count the outcomes with a score of 7 or more for each spinner number (die number needed is at least $7-s$):
$$\begin{aligned} s=1 &: \text{die } 6 &&\text{1 outcome}\\ s=2 &: \text{die } 5, 6 &&\text{2 outcomes}\\ s=3 &: \text{die } 4, 5, 6 &&\text{3 outcomes}\\ s=4 &: \text{die } 3, 4, 5, 6 &&\text{4 outcomes}\end{aligned}$$
There are $1+2+3+4=10$ favourable outcomes.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{score}\ge 7) &= \dfrac{10}{24}\\ &= \dfrac{5}{12} \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

parts.latex:
One hundred tickets are sold in a raffle which offers two prizes. Hazel buys five of the tickets.

A ticket is drawn at random for the first prize. A second ticket is drawn from the remaining tickets for the other prize.

What is the probability that Hazel wins both prizes?

solutions.latex:
Hazel must win the first prize, then the second from the remaining 99 tickets.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{wins both prizes}) &= \dfrac{5}{100}\times\dfrac{4}{99} \\ &= \dfrac{20}{9900} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{495}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Calculates the probability that Hazel wins the first prize, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
There are 8 chocolates in a box. Three have peppermint centres (P) and five have caramel centres (C).

Kim randomly chooses a chocolate from the box and eats it. Sam then randomly chooses and eats one of the remaining chocolates.

A partially completed probability tree is shown.

\exfigure{38_q11_1}

What is the probability that Kim and Sam choose chocolates with different centres?

solutions.latex:
Different centres means Kim chooses P then Sam chooses C, or Kim chooses C then Sam chooses P.

After Kim eats one chocolate, 7 remain.

If Kim chooses P, 2 P and 5 C remain, so $P(\text{C second})=\dfrac{5}{7}$.

If Kim chooses C, 3 P and 4 C remain, so $P(\text{P second})=\dfrac{3}{7}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{different}) &= \dfrac{3}{8}\times\dfrac{5}{7}+\dfrac{5}{8}\times\dfrac{3}{7} \\ &= \dfrac{15}{56}+\dfrac{15}{56} \\ &= \dfrac{15}{28} \end{aligned}$$
So option D is correct.

The second level is left unlabelled, as on the paper. P and C are kept upright as in the question text. The leftover overlay colour is only the smaller fractions and the 0.6pt line weight.

parts.latex:
The top of a rectangular table is divided into 8 equal sections as shown.

\extable{36_q15_t1}

A standard die with faces labelled 1 to 6 is rolled onto the table. The die is equally likely to land in any of the 8 sections of the table. If the die does not land entirely in one section of the table, it is rolled again.

A score is calculated by multiplying the value shown on the top face of the die by the number shown in the section of the table where the die lands.

What is the probability of getting a score of 6?

solutions.latex:
The die is equally likely to land in each of the 8 sections, so each section has probability $\dfrac{1}{8}$. Each face of the die has probability $\dfrac{1}{6}$.

The score is the die value multiplied by the section number. Pairs (section, die) giving a score of 6:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{section } 1 &\text{ and die } 6 \\ \text{section } 2 &\text{ and die } 3 \\ \text{section } 3 &\text{ and die } 2 \\ \text{section } 6 &\text{ and die } 1 \end{aligned}$$
Each section number appears once, so there are 4 such pairs, each with probability $\dfrac{1}{8}\times\dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{48}$.
$$P(\text{score } 6) = 4 \times \dfrac{1}{48} = \dfrac{1}{12}$$
This is option B.

parts.latex:
Two birds are to be randomly released from a birdcage that contains 3 male and 4 female birds.

What is the probability that both released birds are female?

solutions.latex:
There are 7 birds in total, 4 of them female. The birds are released one after the other without replacement.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{both female}) &= \dfrac{4}{7} \times \dfrac{3}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{12}{42} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{7} \end{aligned}$$
This is option A.

figures.cap: lake surrounded by forest with measurements, 350 m by 350 m wide

parts.latex:
A plane is flying through clouds to drop a water quality monitoring system onto a lake.

The lake is surrounded by forest as shown in the diagram, with all measurements in metres.

\exfigure{15_q38_1}

Estimate the probability that the plane will drop the monitoring system onto the lake.

Use the Trapezoidal rule in your calculations.

solutions.latex:
The total area is
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 700 \times 450 \\ &= 315\,000 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Applying the trapezoidal rule with two strips of width $350$ to the lake:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Lake} &\approx \dfrac{350}{2}(80 + 300) + \dfrac{350}{2}(300 + 100) \\ &= 175(380) + 175(400) \\ &\approx 136\,500 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, use $4$ applications of the trapezoidal rule to find the area of the forest, then subtract from the total to obtain $136\,500 \text{ m}^2$.

The probability is the lake area over the total area.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= \dfrac{136\,500}{315\,000} \\ &= \dfrac{13}{30} \approx 43.33\% \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly applies the trapezoidal rule and finds the lake area, or equivalent merit
Correct total area and applies the trapezoidal rule, or equivalent merit
